title: Inheritance
description: Let one class build on another instead of copying its code.

content.real: A child inheriting from a parent
content.concept: A child class built on a parent class
content.text: A `Dog` and a `Cat` both store a name and both eat. Instead of copying that into every animal, write it once in a **parent** class. A **child** class starts with everything the parent has, then adds what makes it different.

items.sub: Holds the shared parts, written once.
Says which parent it builds on, then adds its own extras.

parts.label: child
parts.note: The new class you are writing.

parts.label: parent
parts.note: The parent's name goes in parentheses after the child's name.

content.caption: `Dog` has no `__init__` and no `eat` of its own, and it doesn't need them: both come from `Animal`.

content.question: In `class Cat(Animal):`, which class is the parent?
content.explain: The parent goes in the parentheses. `Cat` is the child that builds on `Animal`.

items: Build a `Dog` object just like any other object.
The parent's `__init__` runs and stores the name.
Call the parent's methods and the child's own methods the same way.
When you call a method, Python looks in the **child first**, then the **parent**.
content.title: How it works

steps.label: Look in `Dog`
steps.detail: The child is checked first. No `eat` here.

content.question: Using the classes above, what does this print?
options: An error: Dog has no eat
content.explain: `Dog` has no `eat`, so Python finds it in the parent `Animal` and runs it with `self.name` as `"Rex"`.

content.value: Press the buttons below to watch that search happen, and notice which box lights up each time.

items: Sometimes the parent's version is wrong for one child.
Write a method with the **same name** in the child.
Python checks the child first, so the child's version wins.
This is called **overriding**. The parent's version is never reached.
content.title: Overriding

items.title: Dog overrides
items.text: Found in `Dog` first, so it prints `Woof!`.

items.title: Cow inherits
items.text: Not in `Cow`, so Python uses `Animal`'s: `Some sound.`

content.value: `pass` is Python's way of saying there is deliberately nothing here. `Cow` inherits everything and adds nothing, and the body of a class or function is never allowed to be empty.
content.title: What is pass?

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `Cat` has its own `speak`, which overrides the parent's. Python checks the child first, so it never reaches `Animal`'s version.

practice.question: Make a Dog called 'rover' and call its eat() method, which Dog inherits from Animal.
Give Cat its own speak() method that prints a meow, so it overrides the one from Animal.

quiz.question: What does a child class get through inheritance?
options: It gets the parent's attributes and methods
It gets a copy that never updates
quiz.explain: The child starts with everything the parent has and can then add its own, without any of the parent's code being copied.

quiz.question: How do you define a class 'Car' that inherits from 'Vehicle'?
quiz.explain: The parent's name goes in parentheses after the child's. Writing it the other way round would make Vehicle the child.

quiz.question: Both Animal and Dog define speak(). Which one runs for a Dog object?
options: Dog's, because Python checks the child class first
Animal's, because the parent always wins
Both of them, one after the other
quiz.explain: Python searches the child first and stops as soon as it finds the method. That is what makes overriding possible.
